items.q: How should a payment system store the amount $49.99?

options.t: As the float 49.99 with the currency code
options.why: Floating point can't represent 0.1 exactly — sum millions of float payments and cents evaporate. Money in floats is an instant interview red flag.

options.t: As the integer 4999 (minor units) with the currency code
options.why: Right. Money is an integer count of the smallest currency unit — 4999 cents. The currency code's exponent tells you yen have no decimals. Integers add exactly; floats don't.

options.t: As the string "49.99" to preserve formatting
options.why: Strings dodge float rounding but you can't do arithmetic or enforce sums in the database. Formatting is a display concern; storage wants exact integers.

options.t: As two columns: dollars and cents
options.why: Workable but clumsy — every sum and comparison needs carry logic, and it breaks for zero-decimal currencies like JPY. One integer of minor units does everything cleanly.

items.q: A retry arrives with an idempotency key you've seen before, and the request hash matches. What does the server do?

options.t: Re-runs the charge but tells the PSP to dedupe it
options.why: Re-execution is exactly what the key exists to prevent. The PSP-side key is a second safety layer, not permission to re-run your own logic.

options.t: Returns 409 Conflict
options.why: 409 is for same key with a DIFFERENT request hash — a confused client. Same key, same hash is the normal retry case and gets the stored response.

options.t: Replays the stored response without re-executing anything
options.why: Yes — byte for byte, whether the original succeeded or failed. A retry must be indistinguishable from its original; that's what makes 'just retry' a safe instruction.

options.t: Creates a second payment intent linked to the first
options.why: That's a sibling charge — the double-charge bug wearing a bookkeeping costume. One key maps to one execution, forever.

items.q: Same idempotency key arrives, but the request body hashes differently than the stored one. Response?

options.t: 409 — the client is confused; refuse to guess
options.why: Right. Same key with different content means the client reused a key for a different request. Executing either interpretation risks losing or double-moving money, so you reject loudly.

options.t: Process the new body — the client clearly updated the order
options.why: You have no idea which version the user meant to pay. 'Clearly' is a guess, and guessing is how money gets lost. The contract is one key = one exact request.

options.t: Replay the stored response anyway
options.why: Now the client thinks their NEW request succeeded when something different executed. Silent mismatches are worse than errors — the client can't even detect the bug.

options.t: Merge the two requests and charge the larger amount
options.why: Inventing money semantics the client never asked for. There is no world where the server picks an amount on its own.

items.q: In a double-entry ledger, what must be true of every transaction's entries?

options.t: They all touch the same account
options.why: Opposite — double-entry means money MOVES between accounts, so a transaction touches at least two: a debit somewhere, a credit somewhere else.

options.t: Their amounts sum to zero
options.why: Exactly. Every cent that leaves one account lands in another; money is never created or destroyed inside the ledger. That zero-sum invariant is what makes bugs structurally detectable.

options.t: They're written by a single dedicated service
options.why: An org choice, not a ledger property. The defining rule is arithmetic: debits and credits balance to zero, whoever writes them.

options.t: Each entry is positive
options.why: Then nothing could balance. Entries carry sign — the debit/credit pair — and it's exactly the mix of + and − that must cancel out.

items.q: You discover a ledger transaction recorded a $5 fee that should have been $4. The correct fix is:

options.t: UPDATE the fee entry from 500 to 400
options.why: Append-only means never updated, never deleted — the application role shouldn't even have the UPDATE grant. An edited ledger can silently rewrite history, which destroys its audit value.

options.t: Delete the bad transaction and re-insert it correctly
options.why: Deletion is the same sin as update: the record now lies about the past. Auditors — and 3 a.m. debuggers — need the error AND its correction visible.

options.t: Append a reversing transaction, then the correct one
options.why: Right. Corrections are new entries that visibly undo the mistake. The error and its fix both stay in the record forever — that's what makes the ledger a flight recorder instead of a whiteboard.

options.t: Adjust the merchant's cached balance to compensate
options.why: The cached balance is a derived view — touching it directly moves money outside the ledger discipline, and the nightly recompute-and-compare job will page someone about exactly this.

items.q: Where does a merchant's balance authoritatively live?

options.t: In a balance column, updated on each payment
options.why: A mutable balance column is a sticky note saying 'about 40 beads' — when it's wrong there's nothing to check it against. It can exist only as a cache of the real answer.

options.t: It's SUM(ledger entries) for their account; any stored balance is a cached view
options.why: Yes. Balances are derived, never authoritative. Cache for speed, recompute nightly for truth, page on divergence — the invariant check is part of the design.

options.t: At the PSP — they hold the money
options.why: The PSP knows what it owes you in aggregate, not each merchant's share of your platform. Your ledger is the source of truth for internal accounting; reconciliation checks it against the PSP.

options.t: In the payouts table
options.why: Payouts record money leaving — one kind of movement. The balance is the sum of ALL movements through the merchant's ledger account.

items.q: Your charge call to the PSP times out. What's the one legal next move?

options.t: Query the PSP by your idempotency key to learn what actually happened
options.why: Right. A timeout puts you in one of three unknowable worlds — never arrived, charged, or still processing. Ambiguity is resolved by asking, never by re-doing.

options.t: Retry immediately — timeouts usually mean the request was lost
options.why: 'Usually' is the trap. In the world where the charge landed and only the response died, a blind retry is a second charge. This exact move is how double-charge incidents are born.

options.t: Mark the payment failed and refund defensively
options.why: You can't refund a charge you're not sure exists, and marking failed when money moved creates a phantom the customer will find on their statement. Query first; act on facts.

options.t: Wait for the webhook to tell you
options.why: Webhooks are the backstop, not the only path — they can be delayed or lost, leaving the intent stuck for hours. The sweeper actively queries by key within minutes.

items.q: What delivery contract should you assume for PSP webhooks?

options.t: Exactly once, in order — PSPs are payment-grade infrastructure
options.why: No network delivers exactly-once-in-order to an external endpoint. Payment-grade means they retry aggressively — which guarantees you duplicates and reordering.

options.t: At least once, in any order
options.why: Yes — you WILL get duplicates and you WILL see refund.succeeded before its payment.succeeded. So: dedupe on event id, apply through the state machine with a version check.

options.t: At most once — some events just won't arrive
options.why: Half right: individual deliveries can fail, but PSPs redeliver until acknowledged. The practical contract is at-least-once — and events CAN still be lost past the retry horizon, which is why reconciliation exists.

options.t: Best effort, so poll instead and ignore webhooks
options.why: Webhooks are the low-latency happy path; polling everything is wasteful and slow. The design uses webhooks + sweeper + reconciliation as layered nets, not either/or.

items.q: How does the design keep raw card numbers off your servers?

options.t: Encrypt card numbers before storing them in Postgres
options.why: Encrypted PANs on your servers still put you in full PCI scope — the fortress-with-quarterly-audits regime. The goal is for card data to never touch your infrastructure at all.

options.t: Hash the card number and store the hash
options.why: A hash can't be used to charge the card later, and the raw number still transited your servers to be hashed. Neither problem is solved.

options.t: Only accept payments through mobile wallets
options.why: Narrows the product, not the compliance answer. Tokenization via the PSP works for plain card entry too.

options.t: PSP-hosted fields: the card number goes browser → PSP directly; you receive and store a token
options.why: Right — same shape as presigned-URL uploads: the sensitive payload skips your servers, you handle only a reference. PCI scope collapses to a questionnaire, and a database breach leaks no card numbers.

items.q: Two identical pay requests (same idempotency key) hit two different app servers in the same millisecond. Trace the outcome.

options.t: Both insert the key, both charge; the PSP's dedupe collapses them to one
options.why: Outsourcing your race condition to the PSP. Their key is the second net, not the first — your unique constraint must prevent two executions from ever starting.

options.t: Both try to insert the key; the unique constraint lets one win, the other blocks on the row lock, then replays or gets 202
options.why: Exactly. One inserts and proceeds; the loser wakes on the lock, sees the key exists, and either replays the finished response or returns 202-in-flight. At no point do two executions run.

options.t: A distributed lock service serializes them before the database
options.why: A whole new infrastructure dependency to solve what a unique constraint plus row lock already solves inside the transaction you needed anyway. Over-engineering with a straight face.

options.t: Last-write-wins on the intent row resolves it
options.why: LWW means both executed and one result got silently discarded — with a real charge possibly behind each. Payments need mutual exclusion before execution, not conflict resolution after.

items.q: Why not wrap the PSP charge call inside the database transaction, so intent and charge commit or abort together?

options.t: It's actually fine if the transaction timeout exceeds the HTTP timeout
options.why: Timeouts don't fix it — the problem is rollback, not timing. No timeout setting makes an external charge reversible by your database.

options.t: Because an HTTP call can't be rolled back: if the txn aborts after the PSP said yes, money moved and your DB remembers nothing
options.why: The dual-write trap in one sentence. External side effects don't obey your transaction. Hence intent-first + outbox: commit what you're about to do, then act, then record the result.

options.t: Because the PSP forbids being called from inside transactions
options.why: The PSP can't see your transactions. The impossibility is structural — two systems, no shared commit — not a vendor policy.

options.t: It works but holds locks too long, so it's a performance issue
options.why: The connection-pool starvation is real but it's the minor charge. The felony is correctness: a rollback after an external success loses track of moved money.

items.q: Your worker crashes after calling the PSP but before recording the outcome. How does the system heal?

options.t: The intent sits in processing past its deadline; the sweeper queries the PSP with the deterministic key and writes what actually happened
options.why: Yes — every crash window has a recovery story because intent precedes action. The sweeper resolves the ambiguity by asking, and the deterministic key (intent_id + attempt) makes the question answerable.

options.t: The database transaction rolls back, undoing the charge
options.why: There's no transaction spanning the PSP — that's the whole dual-write problem. The charge may be real; only a query reveals it.

options.t: The sweeper re-sends the charge; the amounts are reconciled later
options.why: Close but backwards on the crucial step: the sweeper may re-send WITH the same PSP key (safe — they dedupe), but the correct primitive is query-first. 'Charge again and reconcile' as a strategy normalizes creating duplicates.

options.t: The next user retry recreates the intent and starts over
options.why: The retry replays against the existing key — it can't recreate anything, by design. And healing can't depend on the user coming back; the sweeper runs regardless.

items.q: A refund.succeeded webhook arrives for intent p_777, but your DB shows p_777 still in processing. Your handler should:

options.t: Apply it — the PSP is the source of truth for payment outcomes
options.why: Jumping processing → refunded skips succeeded, so settlement ledger entries were never written — the refund now reverses money the ledger never recorded receiving. The state machine exists precisely to block this.

options.t: Discard it as invalid
options.why: It's almost certainly a real event arriving out of order — its sibling payment.succeeded is in flight behind it. Dropping it means the refund never lands. Park, don't discard.

options.t: Refuse the transition; park the event for retry and refetch the intent's current truth from the PSP API
options.why: Right. Illegal transitions are rejected, not forced. Out-of-order delivery resolves in minutes via the parked retry or the refetch, which walks the intent through succeeded-then-refunded with audit events for both.

options.t: Force the state to refunded but log a warning
options.why: A warning log doesn't balance a ledger. Skipped states mean skipped ledger writes — you'd find the hole at reconciliation, the hard way.

items.q: A $50 payment settled earlier as: psp_receivable +5000, merchant_payable −4500, platform_revenue −500. Now refund $20 to the customer (merchant bears it). Which entries are right?

options.t: merchant_payable +2000, psp_receivable −2000
options.why: Sums to zero and reverses direction: the merchant's payable shrinks by $20 and the PSP-side receivable drops by the $20 going back to the card. A mirror of (part of) the original flow.

options.t: psp_receivable −2000
options.why: One-sided — sums to −2000, not zero. Money left the ledger without a source. The zero-sum write check would reject this transaction outright.

options.t: UPDATE the original transaction's amounts down by 2000
options.why: Never update. The original transaction happened; the refund is a NEW movement, appended, that the settlement file will independently confirm.

options.t: refunds_expense +2000, platform_revenue −2000
options.why: Balances to zero, but moves the wrong money: this books the refund against YOUR revenue while the merchant keeps their $45. The entries must trace where the $20 actually comes from — the merchant's payable.

items.q: The daily settlement file contains charge ch_109 for $7.00 — your ledger has no such entry. First move?

options.t: Write a ledger entry for $7.00 so the books match
options.why: Booking money you can't explain hides the bug that lost it. The entry must be produced BY the state machine processing a real object, not typed in to make a report go green.

options.t: Dispute the line with the PSP — you have no record, so it isn't yours
options.why: Your missing record is evidence about YOUR system, not about reality. Real money moved; a lost webhook or a dashboard-made charge is far likelier than PSP fabrication.

options.t: Auto-heal: fetch the charge from the PSP API and drive it through the normal state machine; human queue only if that can't explain it
options.why: Right — orphans are usually lost webhooks or dashboard actions, and the fetch-and-replay path heals them with full audit events. Humans see only the residue machines can't explain.

options.t: Wait a few days — settlement files sometimes contain next-day items
options.why: Backwards: the lag-window grace applies to the OTHER bucket (in your ledger, not yet in the file). Money in the file with no ledger trace is real and unexplained today.

items.q: Your PSP goes hard-down for 30 minutes during normal traffic. With the intent-first design, what actually happens?

options.t: Checkout returns 503 until the PSP recovers — there's nothing to do without them
options.why: The whole point of intent-first is that accepting the order and charging the card are decoupled. Blanket 503s throw away sales the architecture already knows how to save.

options.t: Requests fail over to a second PSP automatically
options.why: Not in this design, deliberately: per-PSP tokenization, a second webhook dialect, doubled reconciliation — a quarter's work bought against a few hours a year. The trigger for revisiting was named; it hasn't fired.

options.t: Intents keep committing; the circuit breaker stops the hammering; the queue drains on recovery — with honest UX about pending payment
options.why: So close — but this is only right for goods where delayed confirmation is acceptable. Missing the second half: for instant digital delivery you fail fast and say so. Grade the full answer.

options.t: Physical goods: queue intents and confirm by email later. Instant digital goods: fail fast honestly. Circuit breaker open either way
options.why: Yes — the architecture buys you the queue, and the product decides per-flow whether 'processing, we'll confirm' is honest or whether only fail-fast is. Pretending success you can't verify is how trust dies.

items.q: A charge attempt failed: card declined. The user enters a different card and pays. What happens to the idempotency keys?

options.t: Reuse everything — same purchase, same keys
options.why: Reusing the stored-response machinery would replay the DECLINE. And sending the same PSP key would make the PSP dedupe the new charge into the old failure. New attempt, new PSP key — on purpose.

options.t: The attempt counter increments, so the PSP key becomes intent_id:2 — a deliberately new charge; the client sends a fresh idempotency key for the new request
options.why: Right. The deterministic PSP key is per-attempt precisely so that retries of one attempt dedupe while a genuinely new attempt (new card, user intent) charges cleanly. Duplicates by accident: impossible. New charges on purpose: easy.

options.t: Idempotency keys are only for network retries — a new card doesn't involve them
options.why: The new request still needs its own key, because ITS timeouts and double-taps need protection too. Every mutating request carries a key; what changes is that this one is fresh.

options.t: Block the second attempt until the first key expires
options.why: Punishing the user with a waiting period for your bookkeeping. Keys scope to a request, not to the order — a new attempt is a new request, available immediately.

items.q: Auth success rate drops from 92% to 71% over ten minutes. Which explanations should be on your mental list?

options.t: A PSP or card-issuer incident, or your own bad deploy — it's the most information-dense payments metric precisely because it catches all three
options.why: Yes. A cliff in auth success is upstream trouble (PSP, issuer outage) or self-inflicted (malformed requests from a deploy). Check your deploy timeline first — it's the one you can roll back.

options.t: Normal nightly variance — auth rates swing with time of day
options.why: Auth rates do drift by hour and geography, but 21 points in ten minutes is a cliff, not a tide. Cliffs have causes.

options.t: Users suddenly having worse cards
options.why: Card quality of your user base changes over months, not minutes. Population explanations can't move a metric this fast.

options.t: The reconciliation job is behind
options.why: Reconciliation is a daily batch comparing settled history — it has no path to affect live authorization outcomes. Different layer entirely.

items.q: Thirty seconds into 'design a payment system,' which sentence proves you've found the crux?

options.t: "The hard part is that my database and the PSP can't share a transaction — every payment is a dual-write across a network that can fail after the money moved. I'll spend most of my time on that seam."
options.why: That's the fire. Idempotency keys, intent-first writes, the poller, reconciliation — everything distinctive about payments exists because of this one seam. Naming it and steering there is the interview.

options.t: "Payments spike on Black Friday, so the hard part is elastic scaling of the charge path."
options.why: Even 10x Black Friday is ~1.2K/sec — one Postgres. Leading with scale on a small-QPS correctness problem tells the interviewer you haven't done the estimate.

options.t: "The hard part is fraud detection — most payment engineering is fighting fraud."
options.why: True of the industry, but you scoped fraud to the PSP in minute one. Naming an out-of-scope crux means the scoping and the agenda disagree.

options.t: "The hard part is global consistency — we'll need multi-region consensus for the ledger."
options.why: The ledger is CP with one writer — deliberately boring. Multi-region consensus is imported difficulty; the native difficulty is the PSP boundary under retries.

items.q: The interviewer asks: 'Would you add a second PSP for resilience?' The senior-calibrated answer is:

options.t: "Yes — never depend on a single vendor for something this critical."
options.why: A principle where a cost-benefit should be. Instant multi-PSP without naming dual-vaulting, a second webhook dialect, and doubled reconciliation reads as never having priced it.

options.t: "No — it's too complicated."
options.why: Right conclusion, no reasoning shown, and no condition under which it flips. Unjustified simplicity grades barely better than unjustified complexity.

options.t: "Not in v1: tokens are vaulted per-PSP, so failover means dual-vaulting, a second webhook dialect, and doubled reconciliation — a quarter's work against a few hours of downtime a year that queue-and-drain already covers. Trigger to revisit: repeated SLO breaches or instant-delivery goods."
options.why: Commit, cost the alternative honestly, show the current design covers the realistic failure, and name the trigger that changes the answer. This question is a trap for over-engineers, and this is the exit.

options.t: "I'd design an abstraction layer over both PSPs now so we can add the second one later cheaply."
options.why: The abstraction IS most of the cost — normalizing two webhook dialects and two settlement formats — paid now, against a need that may never arrive. Speculative generality wearing a prudence costume.

items.q: A candidate opens with: '10M payments/day, so I'll shard the payments DB by user_id across 16 nodes for write throughput.' What should they have said?

options.t: Sharding is right, but by merchant_id — payment queries group by merchant
options.why: Debating the shard key concedes the premise. The premise is wrong: there's no write-throughput problem to shard away.

options.t: "10M/day is ~115/sec, ~1.2K peak — one well-run Postgres with headroom. I'll spend the time on idempotency, the ledger, and reconciliation instead."
options.why: The estimate produces the conclusion, and the conclusion redirects the interview to where the fire is. Saying 'this is small' out loud is the senior filter on this problem.

options.t: Sharding is premature, but plan the shard key now to avoid a painful migration later
options.why: Milder over-engineering, same disease: designing against imaginary load. If payments ever needs sharding you'll migrate with years of warning — meanwhile a partitioned single writer keeps transactions simple, which correctness needs today.

options.t: Correct instinct — payments must never be down, and sharding adds resilience
options.why: Sharding is a throughput tool, not a resilience tool — it multiplies failure surface. Resilience here comes from the synchronous replica and the intent-first recovery story.

items.q: Your idempotency stack has four independent dedupe layers. Why still run a duplicate-charge alarm over PSP-side data?

options.t: You shouldn't — alerting on impossible events trains the on-call to ignore alarms
options.why: Alarm fatigue is real for NOISY alarms. This one fires approximately never — and the day it does, it's the most important page of the year. Silence is its normal state, not its failure mode.

options.t: Because the layers share failure modes, so four layers is really one
options.why: They're genuinely independent — client key, unique constraint, deterministic PSP key, PSP-side dedupe live in different systems. The alarm isn't there because the layers are weak; it's there because 'impossible' is a claim about code you control.

options.t: Because 'structurally impossible' is a claim about your code — and duplicates can be minted below it, on the rails themselves. An invariant without a detector is a belief
options.why: Coinbase 2018: their code double-charged no one; the card networks reprocessed a million transactions and duplicates appeared anyway. The alarm converts your invariant from belief into monitored fact, for the cost of one query.

options.t: For compliance — auditors require duplicate detection controls
options.why: Auditors do like controls, but this reasoning outsources your judgment to them. You'd run this alarm with no auditor on earth — because the alternative is learning about duplicates from Reddit.

items.q: Commit a consistency stance for this system. Which one is right, and why?

options.t: Everything strongly consistent — it's money; eventual consistency is never acceptable
options.why: Overpaying: forcing the order-status page through the CP write path buys nothing (a 2-second-stale 'processing' is invisible) and costs availability everywhere. Blanket strong consistency reads as not knowing where the invariants live.

options.t: Ledger and intents are CP — brief write pause on failover rather than ever forking the money truth. Product surfaces read eventually consistent replicas
options.why: Consistency where invariants live, availability where users look. A forked ledger is unforgivable; a stale status page is invisible. Committing to the split — and to the failover pause — is the senior stance.

options.t: AP everywhere with CRDTs merging concurrent ledger writes
options.why: CRDTs merge by making concurrent updates commute — but 'charge if and only if not already charged' is exactly the non-commutative decision. Money invariants need serialization, not merge functions.

options.t: Consistency level per-request, chosen by the calling service
options.why: Tunable consistency on a ledger means the least careful caller defines your guarantees. The stance must be structural — enforced by the architecture, not by convention.

items.q: 'Now 10x the volume.' What actually strains first in this design?

options.t: Postgres write throughput — time to shard
options.why: 12K/sec on an append-mostly table is still a beefy single-writer with partitioning. Reaching for sharding at 10x repeats the mistake the estimate was supposed to prevent.

options.t: The humans: a review queue growing linearly with volume is a slow-motion outage — the metric to invest in is the auto-heal rate
options.why: Right. The machines scale by config; the reconciliation break queue scales by headcount unless the machine-resolved fraction climbs. That's where the next engineer-year goes — an ops-maturity answer interviewers rarely hear.

options.t: The idempotency key table becomes the bottleneck
options.why: One indexed insert per payment at 12K/sec, with old keys archived past the retry horizon — Postgres shrugs. Plausible-sounding, numerically empty.

options.t: Webhook ingestion needs a Kafka buffer at that volume
options.why: ~2-3 webhook events per payment is ~30K/sec of tiny inserts at peak — within reach of the existing stack, and the webhook path is already async by nature. Adding Kafka here is a reflex, not a need.

items.q: Interviewer: 'Your PSP call times out. Walk me through exactly what happens next.' Which walkthrough passes at E5?

options.t: "The intent's already committed as processing with its key. The worker's timeout fires; the sweeper later finds the overdue row, queries the PSP by intent_id:attempt, and writes whichever truth comes back — charged means proceed to succeeded and ledger entries; not-found means safe re-send with the same key. The user's retry meanwhile replays against the stored key — no second execution."
options.why: Every table, every state, both the machine's path and the user's path, and no step guesses. This level of specificity — mechanism, not vibes — is exactly what the probe is fishing for.

options.t: "We retry with exponential backoff and jitter, capped at three attempts."
options.why: Backoff is a rate policy, not a correctness answer. Without the idempotency key and query-first mechanics, three polite retries can still mean three charges.

options.t: "We return an error and let the user try again — their retry is idempotency-protected."
options.why: Half a system: the user path is safe, but the original charge is still in an unknown state, and nothing here resolves it. The sweeper-and-query half is the part that was actually being probed.

options.t: "Timeouts are rare with a tier-one PSP; we'd alert and investigate manually."
options.why: Timeouts are a WHEN on every network. 'Rare, so manual' means every incident is an engineer spelunking in production — the design was supposed to make this boring and automatic.
